questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presented with recurrent fevers that lasted for 6 days. The episodes were very regular, appearing every 4 weeks. The fever was accompanied by sore throat and mouth ulcers. He was asymptomatic between episodes. There was no significant family history. His C-reactive protein and total white cell count were very elevated during each episode.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis syndrome

questions.explanation: Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis syndrome The regular periodicity of fevers suggests either cyclic neutropenia or PFAPA. This patient’s WBC count is elevated, therefore cyclic neutropenia is unlikely.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q45

2 treatment options
Name 3 other periodic fever syndrome

parts_raw.text: What are 4 classic features of the likely periodic fever syndrome
2 treatment options
Name 3 other periodic fever syndrome

questions.model_answer:
a) PFAPA syndrome: (1) Periodic Fever, clockwork-regular every 3-6 weeks, onset before age 5, each episode 3-6 days; (2) Aphthous stomatitis; (3) Pharyngitis (exudative, culture-negative for group A Streptococcus); (4) Cervical adenitis, with complete well-being, normal growth and no symptoms between episodes.
b) (1) Single dose of prednisone/prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg at fever onset (aborts the attack); (2) Tonsillectomy (curative in most); alternatives include cimetidine or colchicine for prophylaxis.
c) (1) Familial Mediterranean fever; (2) TNF-receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS); (3) Hyper-IgD syndrome/mevalonate kinase deficiency (also cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes).
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell periodic-fever/fever-of-unknown-origin chapters and standard pediatric autoinflammatory disease criteria (Marshall/Thomas criteria for PFAPA).

questions.model_answer:

Empiric treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Early-onset bacterial sepsis/pneumonia: group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli and other gram-negative enterics, Listeria monocytogenes. Congenital infections: syphilis, congenital tuberculosis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella. Perinatal viral infection: disseminated herpes simplex virus, enterovirus/parechovirus. b) Ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside (gentamicin/tobramycin) or cefotaxime, with intravenous acyclovir added if disseminated HSV is a consideration; send blood cultures, maternal and infant syphilis serology, HSV and enterovirus PCR, and give supportive care with surfactant and ventilation.

questions.question: A six-month-old infant with diarrhea has a positive Clostridioides difficile assay.
questions.question_raw: Six month old with diarrhea, C. difficile assay positive.

parts.text: Do you treat?
What is the colonization rate in this age group?
At what age does it equal the adult rate?

parts_raw.text: Do you treat?
What is the colonization rate?
When does it equal the adult rate?

questions.model_answer: a) No. Infants and children up to 1-2 years of age are frequently asymptomatically colonized with toxigenic C. difficile, and the rate of stool positivity in young children with diarrhea is no higher than in those without; testing for CDI is not recommended in this age group and a positive assay should not be treated. b) Colonization is very common: when sampled monthly over the first year of life essentially all infants are colonized at some point with toxigenic and/or nontoxigenic strains. c) Beyond age 3 years the colonization rate resembles that of adults (<3%).
questions.beyond_mandell: The commonly quoted stratified carriage figures (~60% neonates, ~30% infants/toddlers, ~3% over age 2) are not stated in this chapter; the chapter gives only "essentially all colonized at some point in year 1" and adult-equivalent (<3%) beyond age 3.

cohort_answer.text:
No – absence of intestinal receptors for C diff that are necessary to cause infection
15% to 63% of neonates, 3% to 33% of infants and toddlers <2yo, 1-3% of children >2yo are asymptomatic carriers. Remember: 60,30,3
After 2-3 years old, 1-3%

questions.model_answer:
a) CSF pleocytosis - GBS: No (elevated protein with absent/minimal pleocytosis = albuminocytologic dissociation); Polio: Yes (pleocytosis with minimally elevated protein).
Symmetrical - GBS: Yes (symmetrical bilateral ascending paralysis); Polio: No (characteristically asymmetrical).
Sensation loss - GBS: Yes; Polio: No (sensory loss is very rare and should suggest another diagnosis).
b) (1) Enterovirus A71. (2) Enterovirus D68. (Also West Nile virus.)
c) (1) Throat secretions - virus usually isolated in the first week of illness. (2) Feces - virus shed often for several weeks. (3) CSF - poliovirus is rarely isolated from CSF, but a CNS isolate is especially valuable for evaluating vaccine-associated paralytic polio. (4) Paired acute and convalescent sera for type-specific neutralizing antibody when no isolate is available.
d) Anterior horns of the spinal cord (motor neurons of the gray matter).
e) Cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal) and X (vagus).

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Localized skin, eye and mouth disease (vesicular skin lesions, keratoconjunctivitis/chorioretinitis, oral ulcers); (2) CNS disease/encephalitis; (3) Disseminated visceral disease presenting as neonatal sepsis with hepatitis, pneumonitis and adrenal involvement. Note many infants have no visible skin lesions until late in the course.
b) High — 30% to 50% when the mother acquires HSV near term; risk is further increased by HSV-1 rather than HSV-2 (OR 35), cervical rather than vulvar shedding (OR 15) and fetal scalp electrodes (OR 3.5).
c) Very low. Reactivation at delivery carries <1% transmission, and abdominal delivery is protective (OR 0.14); an infant delivered by cesarean before rupture of membranes is at minimal risk.
d) A septic-appearing neonate has disseminated HSV disease; regardless of maternal stage, evaluate immediately (surface PCR/cultures, blood and CSF HSV PCR, liver enzymes) and start empirical high-dose IV acyclovir before results return, since untreated neonatal herpes carries 65% mortality.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Blood cultures (candidemia/dissemination). (2) Lumbar puncture — CNS involvement is more frequent in neonates with candidemia, and LP should be considered whenever an infant's blood cultures grow Candida. (3) Dilated funduscopic/retinal examination for ocular candidiasis (plus consider renal/abdominal ultrasound).
b) Amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg IV daily.
c) It is well tolerated with low nephrotoxicity in neonates, achieves good CNS and urinary-tract penetration (neonates are at high risk of CNS dissemination), whereas echinocandins penetrate CNS/urine poorly with limited neonatal data, and fluconazole is less favoured here.
d) Remove the PICC/central catheter — catheter removal is almost always required for cure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Neonatal first-line AmB deoxycholate and its rationale are from the 2016 IDSA candidiasis guideline; the chapter does not specify neonatal treatment.

questions.question_raw: Treatment of C. Diff (can only use a regimen once).

parts.text: 8 month old

40 year old with first non-severe episode

parts_raw.text: 8 month old

50 year old with fulminant colitis and ileus

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old: do not treat-infants are commonly colonized and a positive test does not mean CDI; confirm true infection and provide supportive care only. b) 13-year-old, second recurrence: fecal microbiota transplantation (appropriate after adequate antibiotic treatment of >=2 recurrences); alternatively vancomycin taper-and-pulse or vancomycin followed by rifaximin. c) 50-year-old, fulminant with ileus: oral/NG vancomycin 500 mg qid PLUS IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h, add rectal vancomycin enema if complete ileus, with early surgical consult. d) 40-year-old, first non-severe: fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x10 d (or oral vancomycin 125 mg qid x10 d).

cohort_answer.text: 8 month old: ensure true C. diff (infants <12 months often colonized); if treated, can use same regimen as adults (vancomycin) with adjusted dose. 13yo second recurrence: strongest recommendation/evidence for fecal transplant; otherwise treated similarly to first recurrence (pulse/tapering vancomycin); option to use rifaximin for 20 days after initial vancomycin (fidaxomicin never gets a taper). 50yo fulminant colitis and ileus: Vancomycin PO + Metronidazole (Flagyl) IV. 40yo first non-severe episode: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days; Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x10 days; or metronidazole as a weak alternative x10 days at TID dosing.

questions.question: A 21-month-old child has discitis.
questions.question_raw: 21 wk old with discitis.

parts.text: What are the two top organisms?
Why is discitis less common in a 7-year-old?

parts_raw.text: What are two top organisms?
Why do 7 year-old have less common discitis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus. (2) Kingella kingae.
b) The intervertebral disk of a young child is still perfused by vascular channels crossing the vertebral end plate, allowing hematogenous seeding. These channels involute by about 7-8 years of age, leaving the disk avascular and no longer seedable during bacteraemia, so infection at that age presents instead as vertebral osteomyelitis.
questions.beyond_mandell: The vascular-involution explanation is pediatric-literature based (CPS osteoarticular infection statement 2018), not stated in Mandell.

questions.model_answer:
a) About 0.5% of live births (roughly 1 in 200 in the US; prevalence ~6 per 1000, higher [>10/1000] in South America, Asia, and Africa).
b) (1) Petechial rash/hepatosplenomegaly with jaundice. (2) Microcephaly (with chorioretinitis, seizures).

cohort_answer.text:
0.5-1% of all live borne infants infected in utero (Red Book)
Clinical manifestations: General (IUGR, prematurity); Skin (petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, jaundice); Hematopoietic (thrombocytopenia, anemia, splenomegaly); Hepatobiliary (hyperbilirubinemia, elevated ALT, hepatomegaly); CNS (microcephaly, seizures, periventricular calcifications, brain malformation); Eye (chorioretinitis, strabismus, optic atrophy, microphthalmia); Ear (SNHL)

questions.question: Pediatric spinal infections.
questions.question_raw: Pediatric spinal infections

parts.text: Why is discitis not as commonly seen in children older than 7?
What are the two most common organisms to which antibiotic therapy should be tailored?

parts_raw.text: A) Why is discitis not as commonly seen in kids older than 7?
B) What are the 2 most common organisms to which antibiotic tx should be tailored?

questions.model_answer:
a) Because the vascular anatomy of the disc changes with age. In young children the intervertebral disc is richly vascularized by vessels crossing the cartilaginous vertebral end plate into the anulus, so transient bacteremia seeds the disc itself; these intraosseous/transdiscal vessels progressively involute and are obliterated by about 7 to 10 years of age, leaving only a peripheral anastomotic network. After that age hematogenous seeding lodges in the vertebral body metaphyseal equivalent rather than the disc, so infection presents as vertebral osteomyelitis/spondylodiscitis rather than isolated discitis.
b) (1) Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA, a recognized cause of discitis in children). (2) Kingella kingae, particularly in children under about 4 years.
questions.beyond_mandell: The age-related involution of the vertebral end-plate/disc vessels is pediatric orthopedic-infection teaching (Feigin/Mandell pediatric osteomyelitis literature); Chapter 104 states only that hematogenous disc-space seeding occurs and names S. aureus and K. kingae as leading pediatric pathogens.

cohort_answer.text:
Unlike adults, intervertebral disc in children is richly vascularized (vessels across cartilaginous vertebral plate into ring). After age 8 these vessels disappear but a rich anastomotic network remains peripherally. Rich vasculature <7 years enables bacterial emboli deposition within disc with possible extension to endplates/vertebral bodies
S. aureus; Kingella kingae

questions.question: A mother is diagnosed with syphilis and her baby is asymptomatic at birth. For each of the following maternal-treatment scenarios, state how you would manage the neonate.
questions.question_raw: Congenital syphilis. Baby asymptomatic.

parts.text: Mother treated at 37 weeks with a single dose of IM penicillin.
Mother treated early with IM penicillin x 3 doses; maternal RPR fell from 1:64 to 1:2; baby's RPR is 1:2.
Mother treated early with maternal RPR falling from 1:32 to 1:2; baby's RPR is undetectable.

parts_raw.text: A) Mom treated at 37 weeks IM pen x 1
B) Mom treated early with IM penicillin x 3. RPR 1:64 dropped to 1:2. Baby RPR 1:2
C) Mom treated early 1:32 to 1:2. Baby undetectable

questions.model_answer: a) Treatment completed <4 weeks before delivery is considered inadequate, so the infant is classified as probable congenital syphilis regardless of the normal exam. Perform full evaluation (quantitative non-treponemal test, CBC/platelets, CSF for VDRL/cell count/protein, long-bone radiographs, and audiology/ophthalmology/LFTs as indicated) and treat with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IV q12h for the first 7 days then q8h to complete 10 days (or procaine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM daily x 10 days). b) Mother adequately treated early with an appropriate (>4-fold) decline in titre, and baby's RPR (1:2) is not 4-fold higher than the mother's: congenital infection is unlikely. Baseline exam plus serologic follow-up; a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM may be given if follow-up is uncertain. c) Mother adequately treated early with >4-fold titre decline and baby non-reactive: lowest risk. Clinical and serologic follow-up alone, with non-treponemal titres expected to be non-reactive by 6 months; treat only if titres rise or the infant becomes symptomatic.
questions.beyond_mandell: The scenario-specific neonatal evaluation and the 4-fold titre/4-week treatment thresholds and serologic follow-up schedule are from the CDC/AAP congenital syphilis algorithm; Mandell supplies the 'inadequately treated' definition and the CS penicillin regimen.

cohort_answer.text:
Because mom was treated within 4 weeks of delivery, considered inadequate. Requires full work up: syphilis serology, LP with cell count/VDRL/protein (as clinically indicated: long bones x-ray, audiology, ophtho). Treat baby with Pen G 50,000U/kg IV q12h x first 7d then q8h for total 10 days
Since mom was treated before 4 weeks from delivery, and baby is asymptomatic, unlikely congenital syphilis. Presumably late latent treatment; baseline and monthly exams for 3 months with serology @0,3,6,18 months. No further assessment unless becomes symptomatic or RPR higher than mom's or does not resolve. RPR should trend down by 3 months, nonreactive at 6 months. Treponemal tests negative by 12-18 months
Over 4-fold decrease in titer and treated early. If no risk of reinfection and titer remains low and baby titer not 4-fold above mom's, do baseline with monthly exams for 3 months and serology @0,3,6,18 months

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis rests on a combination of maternal, clinical and laboratory criteria: an infant born to a mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis at delivery; a reactive infant treponemal test; direct detection of T. pallidum (darkfield microscopy, PCR, or silver/immunohistochemical staining) from lesion exudate, placenta, umbilical cord, or nasal discharge; plus supporting findings - clinical signs (hepatosplenomegaly, rash, jaundice, anemia), long-bone radiographic changes, abnormal CSF cell count/protein, reactive CSF VDRL, or a reactive IgM test. b) Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IV q12h for the first 7 days of life then q8h for a total of 10 days, or procaine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM daily for a minimum of 10 days. c) (1) Mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis at delivery; (2) Mother treated with a non-penicillin regimen; (3) Inadequate maternal serologic response (<4-fold decline in titre) or treatment not documented; (4) Syphilitic stillbirth (fetal death after 20 weeks with untreated/inadequately treated mother) or clinical signs of syphilis in the infant.
questions.beyond_mandell: The 'treated within 4 weeks of delivery' criterion and abnormal placenta/cord prompt are from CDC guidance; Mandell grounds the other situations (inadequate/absent maternal treatment, non-penicillin therapy, stillbirth >20 weeks, infant signs).

cohort_answer.text:
Maternal syphilis screening in first trimester; repeat at 28-32 weeks and delivery if high risk. In CSF always send VDRL not RPR, repeat every 6 mo until negative if initial positive
Maternal: Primary/secondary/early latent - benzathine penicillin G 2.4mU IM x1 dose. Late latent - benzathine pen G 2.4mU IM weekly x3 weeks. Infant: Crystalline penG IV 50,000U/kg q12h x first 7d then q8h for total 10 days
Signs/symptoms present in baby; Abnormal placenta/cord (barber's pole spiral stripes); Mom treated with non-PCN antibiotic; Mom treated within 4 weeks of delivery or inadequately treated; <4 fold titer decline or not documented; Relapse/doubts about adequacy of treatment or reinfection; Adequacy of infant follow-up cannot be assured and mom treated before pregnancy; Stillborn >20 weeks

questions.question: A mother has a negative RPR (non-treponemal) but a positive treponemal test (EIA) and is treated with 3 doses of penicillin over 3 weeks. She is retested prior to delivery and her RPR is now 1:16.
questions.question_raw: Congenital syphilis: Mom RPR (Non-Treponemal) negative, treponemal test + (EIA), treated with 3 doses of penicillin x 3 weeks. Retested prior to delivery, now RPR is 1:16

parts.text: Most likely explanation for the negative non-treponemal assay initially.
What to do for the baby?
List four radiographic or laboratory findings.
Likelihood of syphilis infection if first- or second-stage maternal disease.
The baby's treponemal serology is positive but RPR is negative. What will you do now and how will you follow?

parts_raw.text: A) Most likely explanation for negative assay initially
B) What to do for baby?
C) 4 radiographical or lab findings
D) Likelihood of syphilis infections if first or second stage
E) Baby's syphilis serology +, RPR negative. What will you do now, how will you follow?

questions.model_answer: a) Early primary infection: non-treponemal (RPR) tests lack sensitivity early and are non-reactive in roughly 30% of early primary cases, whereas treponemal tests become reactive 1-2 weeks after the chancre and remain reactive for life; the rising RPR (now 1:16) reflects evolving/under-treated infection or reinfection. b) Evaluate the infant: quantitative RPR/VDRL compared to the mother (should be <4-fold of maternal titre) and full physical exam; if the infant titre is 4-fold greater than the mother's or the exam is abnormal, treat as proven/highly probable congenital syphilis with penicillin G x 10 days; if reinfection is suspected, full workup with empiric treatment. c) (1) Reactive CSF VDRL; (2) CSF pleocytosis and/or elevated protein; (3) Long-bone radiographic changes (metaphyseal lucency/periostitis); (4) Thrombocytopenia or anemia. d) Vertical transmission is highest with untreated primary/secondary (early) maternal syphilis, approaching 60-100%, with substantial risk of stillbirth and perinatal death; risk falls with later maternal stage. e) A positive treponemal test in the infant most likely reflects passively transferred maternal IgG; repeat the treponemal test at 15-18 months (should become non-reactive if uninfected) and repeat the RPR at ~3 months to exclude incubating congenital syphilis - treat if either remains/becomes reactive.
questions.beyond_mandell: Stage-specific vertical-transmission percentages, the specific radiographic signs (e.g. Wimberger sign, metaphyseal osteochondritis), and the timed infant serologic follow-up (persistence of maternal treponemal antibody to ~15-18 months) derive from CDC/epidemiologic data; Mandell grounds the serologic explanation, CS criteria and treatment.

cohort_answer.text:
Early primary infection - non-treponemal tests become positive 4-6 weeks after infection while treponemal tests become positive earlier and once positive most remain positive despite tx. OR reinfection (consider especially if high risk)
Test baby for RPR/VDRL to ensure titer is 4x less and not greater than mom; infant physical exam. If abnormal to either, baby has proven or highly probable congenital syphilis and treat with PenG x10 days IV. If mom high risk (possible reinfection), full workup with empiric treatment
Lab: CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose); VDRL+ in CSF; Thrombocytopenia; anemia. Radiographic: Symmetrical long bone lesions; Metaphyseal osteochondritis; Wimberger's sign; Diaphyseal periostitis; Osteitis (celery stick appearance); Dactylitis
Vertical transmission depends on maternal stage: Primary/Secondary untreated 70-100% (25% stillbirth, 14% neonatal death, 41% congenital infection, 20% healthy). Early latent 40%. Late latent 10%
Treponemal antibody may remain positive up to 15 months postnatally (maternal Abs), repeat at 18 months should be negative. Repeat RPR at 3 months to rule out incubating congenital syphilis. If positive at all for both, baby warrants tx for congenital syphilis

parts_raw.text: A) % of children that are infected (of women who seroconverted just before or during pregnancy)

questions.model_answer:
a) With primary maternal infection during pregnancy, intrauterine transmission occurs in approximately 30% overall (first-trimester infection carries a lower transmission rate but more severe fetal disease).
b) About 10-15% of congenitally infected infants are symptomatic at birth; ~30% of symptomatic infants develop long-term neurodevelopmental sequelae, and hearing loss can occur even in initially asymptomatic infants.
c) (1) Microcephaly. (2) Hepatosplenomegaly. (3) Petechial rash/jaundice (chorioretinitis, seizures and IUGR also occur).
d) (1) Sensorineural hearing loss (most frequent sequela). (2) Neurodevelopmental delay.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives trimester-specific transmission (T1 34.8%); Mandell states ~30% overall for primary infection and notes first-trimester infection is less frequently transmitted but more severe.

cohort_answer.text:
Vertical transmission by timing: Pre-gestational 0%; Peri-conceptional 4.6%; First trimester 34.8%; Second trimester 42.0%; Third trimester 58.6%; Overall gestational 39.9%
17-20% of congenitally infected infants have permanent sequelae; 9.5% have isolated hearing impairment (1/3 symptomatic at birth). Of 1000 infants: 127 symptomatic (12.7%, 5 deaths, 50-70 with permanent sequelae 40-58%); 873 asymptomatic (5 deaths 0.7%, 118 with permanent sequelae 13.5%)
Clinical manifestations: General (IUGR, prematurity); Skin (petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, jaundice); Hematopoietic (thrombocytopenia, anemia, splenomegaly); Hepatobiliary; CNS (microcephaly, seizures, periventricular calcifications); Eye; Ear (SNHL). Immediately perform CMV testing if microcephaly, hydrops, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, chorioretinitis, ventricular/periventricular calcifications
Hearing loss (27-69%); Microcephaly (35-40%); Cognitive deficits (50-70%); Visual impairment (22-58%)

questions.question: Congenital varicella.
questions.question_raw: Congenital varicella

parts.text: What are the characteristic clinical findings of congenital varicella?
A pregnant woman early in gestation is exposed to chickenpox. What is the risk to the baby of VZV embryopathy, and what are the clinical manifestations of VZV embryopathy?

parts_raw.text: A) What are the characteristic clinical findings of congenital varicella?
B) Pregnant woman early in gestation exposed to chickenpox. What is the risk to baby of VZV embryopathy and what are the clinical manifestations of VZV embryopathy?

questions.model_answer:
a) Congenital varicella syndrome is characterized by cicatricial skin scarring, hypoplastic (limb) extremities, eye abnormalities (cataracts, chorioretinitis, microphthalmia), and CNS impairment (cortical atrophy, seizures, intellectual disability); intrauterine growth restriction is also seen.
b) If the mother is immune there is no risk. In a susceptible woman, the risk of embryopathy is low: roughly 0.4% with maternal infection before 12 weeks, rising to ~2% between weeks 13-20, and rare beyond 20 weeks. Manifestations are as in part (a): limb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin scarring, ocular defects (cataracts, chorioretinitis, microphthalmia), and CNS damage (cortical atrophy, intellectual disability, seizures).
questions.beyond_mandell: The trimester-specific risk figures (0.4% <12 wk, ~2% at 13-20 wk) are from Paryani/Arvin and standard obstetric ID references; this chapter describes the syndrome but not the exact percentages.

cohort_answer.text:
IUGR; Cicatrical (scarring) skin lesions; Ocular deficits (cataracts, chorioretinitis, micro-ophthalmos, nystagmus); Limb hypoplasia; CNS (cortical atrophy, seizures, intellectual disability)
If mom immune, no concerns. If non-immune: incidence of congenital abnormalities 0.4% if maternal infection before 12th week, increases to ~2% between weeks 13-20. Rarely occurs beyond 20 weeks

questions.question: A neonate from Nunavut has miliary tuberculosis.
questions.question_raw: Neonate from Nunavut has military (miliary) TB

parts.text: Give 2 ways he may have acquired it.
How can you tell how he got it?
What is the treatment if he is breastfeeding?
What else can you do?
All cultures are negative including TB. A biopsy shows granuloma. What other organisms can present like this?

parts_raw.text: A) 2 ways that he may have acquired it?
B) How can you tell how he got it?
C) What is Rx if he is breastfeeding?
D) What else can you do?
E) All cultures are negative including TB. A biopsy shows granuloma. What other organisms can present like this?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Congenital (in utero) infection: transplacental hematogenous spread via the umbilical vein, or aspiration/ingestion of infected amniotic fluid. (2) Postnatal airborne transmission from an infectious contact (e.g., the mother or household member).
b) Examine the placenta (histology, smear and culture) and evaluate/screen the mother for active TB (including endometrial/genital TB); congenital disease is supported by a primary hepatic complex or lesions/positive placenta, whereas a well-baby with a later-infectious contact favours postnatal acquisition.
c) Treat the infant with INH, RIF, PZA and EMB plus pyridoxine (B6); disseminated/miliary disease warrants an extended course. If the mother has active TB and the infant does not, give the infant INH plus B6 as prophylaxis and separate mother and infant until she is on effective treatment and non-infectious (approximately 2 weeks).
d) Full evaluation: clinical exam, TST (often negative initially) and/or IGRA, chest radiograph, HIV testing, and appropriate cultures (blood, urine, CSF via lumbar puncture); imaging such as abdominal and head ultrasound.
e) Granulomatous mimics with negative TB cultures: histoplasmosis and other endemic fungi (e.g., blastomycosis); disseminated M. bovis-BCG; Listeria monocytogenes (granulomatosis infantiseptica); nocardiosis; congenital syphilis; and non-infectious granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoidosis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Routes of congenital/neonatal TB acquisition, infant INH prophylaxis dosing, and mother-infant separation are from Red Book/pediatric TB guidance; this chapter covers miliary TB and the granulomatous differential (histoplasmosis, sarcoidosis) but not neonatal acquisition specifics.

cohort_answer.text:
Congenital TB: hematogenous (transplacentally), or aspiration of amniotic fluid. Neonatal TB: airborne transmission
Check placental histology, smears and cultures
Start RIPE, longer duration for miliary/disseminated/bone-joint/CNS (9-12 months). If mom has active TB and baby doesn't: INH 10-15mg/kg + B6 for baby; separate mother and child until mom clinically improving and non-infectious (at least 2 weeks)
Clinical examination; TST (usually negative initially); chest radiography; HIV testing; appropriate cultures (blood, urine, CSF via LP); abdominal and head ultrasound
Histoplasmosis; Blastomycosis; Listeria monocytogenes (granulomatosis infantiseptica); Disseminated mycobacterium bovis (BCG strain); Pulmonary nocardiosis; Syphilis (gummatous disease)

questions.question: A 21-week-old infant with discitis.
questions.question_raw: 21 week old with discitis

parts.text: What are the top two organisms?
Why does a child under 7 years more commonly have discitis?

parts_raw.text: What are the top 2 organisms?
Why does a 7 year old more commonly have discitis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus. (2) Kingella kingae (typically under 4 years, often under 2); in a very young infant, group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli - the organisms of neonatal sepsis - are also important considerations.
b) Young children have a richly vascularized intervertebral disc, with vessels crossing the cartilaginous vertebral end plate; hematogenous seeding during bacteremia therefore deposits in the disc first rather than in bone. Kingella kingae colonizes the posterior pharynx of young children and invades during viral respiratory illness. These transdiscal vessels involute by about 7 to 10 years of age, after which discitis becomes rare.
questions.beyond_mandell: Kingella pharyngeal colonization and age-related disc vascular involution come from pediatric osteoarticular infection literature, not Chapter 104.

cohort_answer.text:
S. aureus; Kingella kingae (less than 4 years, usually under 2)
Children more commonly colonized with Kingella in posterior pharynx - can lead to discitis/OM especially during respiratory infections. Intervertebral discs highly vascularized in children, easily hematogenously seeded. Blood vessels present in cartilaginous vertebral endplate until ~7 years, causing disc infection first rather than bone; after 10 years vessels obliterated

questions.model_answer: a) Renal/bladder ultrasound — to exclude obstructive uropathy or a structural abnormality in a young child (<2 years) with a febrile UTI; abnormal findings (e.g., suspected high-grade reflux) prompt VCUG and urology involvement. b) 7 to 14 days for a febrile UTI (IV if seriously ill, stepping down to oral on response). c) No — no prophylaxis with a normal ultrasound; prophylaxis is reserved for congenital anomaly such as high-grade (grade IV-V) vesicoureteral reflux with scarring.

If RBUS normal, treat 7-10 days

parts.text: What is the treatment?
What test?
When to start?

Safe to breastfeed?

parts_raw.text: What is the treatment?
What test?
When to start
What treatments in baby with timing?
Does the baby need follow up?
Safe to breastfeed?

questions.model_answer: a) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), the preferred nucleos(t)ide analogue in pregnancy; lamivudine is an alternative. b) Maternal HBV DNA quantification (after confirming HBsAg early in pregnancy, with HBeAg/anti-HBe and ALT to stage disease). c) Start in the third trimester (24-32 weeks) if HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL; women with active liver disease meeting treatment criteria are managed as non-pregnant women. d) The baby should receive HBIG and hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, with further vaccine doses at 1 and 6 months. e) Yes: test the infant for HBsAg and anti-HBs after completing the vaccine series (about 1-4 months after the last dose) to confirm they are uninfected and immune. f) Yes, breastfeeding is safe/not contraindicated in a mother on appropriate therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Infant post-vaccination serologic testing timing and the safety of breastfeeding are from AASLD/perinatal guidelines; the chapter states the HBIG + vaccine schedule and TDF preference but not these two specifics.

cohort_answer.text: A) TDF is preferred: "Because it has extensive safety data and a lack of resistance in HBV, TDF is the preferred NA for pregnant women and those with child-bearing potential." B) HBsAg in the first trimester. Those documented to be HBsAg positive require subsequent testing for HBeAg, anti-Hbe, HBV DNA quantification, ALT to assess their stage of disease. C) Typically start at 24-32 weeks to prevent MTCT transmission; start earlier if risk factors for preterm labor, multiple gestations, planned invasive procedures (amnio); start in 2nd trimester if high viral load (>10^9). Pregnant women with HBV DNA of more than 200,000 IU/mL should initiate antiviral therapy at 24-32 weeks (~28 weeks) of gestation to reduce the risk of vertical transmission; may stop at delivery or up to 12 weeks postpartum if given strictly to prevent MTCT. D) Baby should receive HBIg and HBV vaccine within 12h of birth (with second and third doses of vaccine at 1 and 6 months). E) Yes - follow up vaccine dose 2 and 3 at 1 and 6 months respectively. Babies should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs between 1 and 4 months after the last dose of vaccine to confirm that they are uninfected and immune. Check Baby's sAg and sAb; if positive, baby is infected with HBV. If negative but not immune, vaccinate again with 2 additional doses until sAb >10 (immune). F) Yes as long as mom's nipples aren't cracking. Hep B is found in breastmilk but even pre-vaccine era was not associated with transmission. C section not recommended, no effect on MTCT.

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old: no CDI treatment or testing — children <1-2 years are routinely colonized with toxigenic C. difficile and stool positivity does not indicate disease; evaluate for other causes. b) 13-year-old, second recurrence: vancomycin taper-and-pulse regimen (weight-based pediatric dosing). c) 50-year-old, fulminant (fevers, ileus, shock): vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG qid PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h, plus rectal vancomycin (500 mg in 100 mL saline q6h) if complete ileus; early surgical consultation. d) 45-year-old, second recurrence: vancomycin 125 mg PO qid x 10 d followed by rifaximin 400 mg PO tid x 20 d (alternatively fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x 10 d, or fecal microbiota transplantation after at least two recurrences).
questions.beyond_mandell: Pediatric weight-based dosing is not specified in this chapter; peds dosing from guideline sources.

cohort_answer.text:
8 month old: No treatment indicated (should not test in those <2, as routine colonizer that doesn't cause disease). [Note: less toxin receptors in neonatal colons, maternal Ab, different microbiome.]
13M second recurrence: Vancomycin 40mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses (10mg/kg/dose, max 125mg/dose) x10-14 days, then 10mg/kg/dose BID x7 days, then 10mg/kg/dose once daily x7 days, then 10mg/kg/dose q2-3 days x2-8 weeks.
50yo fevers, ileus, shock: Vancomycin 500mg PO/NG QID + Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h + rectal instillation of vancomycin (if ileus present).
45yo second recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO qid x10 days followed by Rifaximin 400mg TID x20 days; OR Vancomycin 125mg PO qid x10-14 days, then BID x7 days, then once daily x7 days, then 125mg PO q2-3 days x2-8 weeks; OR Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x10 days; OR Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x5 days then 200mg PO EOD x20 days; OR Fecal Microbiota Transplantation.
